paragraphs: A PARABLE

The sexton stood in the porch of the Milford meetinghouse, pulling vigorously on the bell rope. The village’s old people came stooping along the street. Bright-faced children skipped happily beside their parents or copied a more solemn walk, conscious of the dignity of their Sunday clothes. Smartly dressed bachelors glanced sideways at the pretty young women and imagined that Sunday sunshine made them prettier than on weekdays. When most of the crowd had streamed into the porch, the sexton began tolling the bell, keeping his eye on the Reverend Mr. Hooper’s door. The first glimpse of the minister was the signal to stop calling people to worship.
“But what has good Parson Hooper got over his face?” the sexton cried in astonishment.

Everyone within earshot immediately turned. They saw what looked like Mr. Hooper walking slowly and thoughtfully toward the meetinghouse. They all started, more surprised than if some strange minister had arrived to shake the dust from the cushions of Mr. Hooper’s pulpit.
“Are you sure that’s our minister?” Goodman Gray asked the sexton.

“Certainly it’s good Mr. Hooper,” the sexton replied. “He was supposed to exchange pulpits with Parson Shute of Westbury, but yesterday Parson Shute sent his apologies. He has a funeral sermon to preach.”

The cause of all this astonishment may seem slight enough. Mr. Hooper was a gentlemanly man of about thirty, still unmarried, dressed with a clergyman’s proper neatness. He looked as though a careful wife had starched his neckband and brushed the week’s dust from his Sunday clothes. Only one thing about his appearance was remarkable. Wrapped around his forehead and hanging over his face, low enough for his breath to stir it, was a black veil. Seen more closely, it appeared to consist of two folds of crepe that completely hid his features except his mouth and chin. It probably did no more to obstruct his vision than darken the appearance of everything, living or lifeless. With this gloomy covering before him, good Mr. Hooper walked slowly and quietly onward. He stooped a little and looked at the ground, as people lost in thought often do, yet nodded kindly to the parishioners still waiting on the steps. They were so astonished that hardly anyone returned his greeting.
“I can’t quite believe good Mr. Hooper’s face is behind that piece of crepe,” said the sexton.
“I don’t like it,” muttered an old woman as she hobbled into the meetinghouse. “Just by hiding his face, he’s turned himself into something dreadful.”
“Our minister has gone mad!” Goodman Gray cried, following him across the threshold.

Rumors of something inexplicable had reached the meetinghouse ahead of Mr. Hooper, stirring the whole congregation. Few could resist twisting their heads toward the door. Many stood up and turned right around, while several little boys climbed onto the seats and came down again with a tremendous clatter. Everyone bustled, women’s dresses rustling and men’s feet shuffling, utterly unlike the hushed stillness that should greet the minister’s entrance. Mr. Hooper seemed not to notice their disturbance. He entered almost silently, gently inclined his head toward the pews on either side, and bowed as he passed his oldest parishioner, a white-haired great-grandfather seated in an armchair in the middle of the aisle. It was strange how slowly this venerable man noticed anything unusual about his pastor. He did not seem fully to share the general astonishment until Mr. Hooper climbed the stairs and stood in the pulpit, face-to-face with his congregation except for the black veil. That mysterious symbol was never lifted. It trembled with his measured breathing as he announced the psalm. It cast its darkness between him and the holy page as he read the Scriptures. During prayer it lay heavily over his upturned face. Was he trying to hide that face from the fearsome Being he addressed?

This simple piece of crepe had such an effect that more than one sensitive woman had to leave the meetinghouse. Yet perhaps the congregation’s pale faces were almost as frightening to the minister as his black veil was to them.

Mr. Hooper was known as a good preacher, though not a forceful one. He tried to draw his people toward heaven with gentle persuasion, rather than drive them there with the thunder of the Word. This sermon had the same style and manner as his usual preaching. Yet something, either in its ideas or in his listeners’ imaginations, made it by far the most powerful sermon they had ever heard him give. It was colored a little more darkly than usual by the gentle gloom of his nature. His subject was secret sin and those sad mysteries we hide from the people nearest and dearest to us, which we would like to hide even from our own awareness, forgetting that the All-Knowing can see them. A subtle power breathed through his words. Everyone, from the most innocent girl to the most hardened man, felt as if the preacher had crept up behind his dreadful veil and discovered their hidden stores of wicked deeds or thoughts. Many pressed their clasped hands against their chests. There was nothing terrible in his words—at least, nothing violent—yet his listeners shook at every tremor of his mournful voice. Unforced tenderness and sorrow went hand in hand with awe. The congregation felt something so unfamiliar in their minister that they longed for a breath of wind to lift the veil. They almost believed a stranger’s face would be revealed, though the body, gestures, and voice were Mr. Hooper’s.

At the end of the service, people hurried outside in an unseemly jumble, eager to share their pent-up astonishment. They felt lighter the moment they lost sight of the black veil. Some huddled in little circles, their mouths whispering together at the center. Others went home alone, lost in silent thought. Some talked loudly and violated the Sabbath with showy laughter. A few shook their wise heads, hinting that they could see through the mystery. One or two insisted there was no mystery: Mr. Hooper had merely weakened his eyes by lamplight at midnight and needed to shade them.

A little later, good Mr. Hooper came out behind his flock. Turning his veiled face from group to group, he paid proper respect to the gray-haired elders. He greeted the middle-aged with the kindly dignity of a friend and spiritual guide, the young with authority and affection, and laid his hands on the small children’s heads to bless them. This was always his Sunday custom. Strange, bewildered looks were his reward. No one sought the honor of walking beside the pastor as they had before. Old Squire Saunders—doubtless through an accidental lapse of memory—failed to invite Mr. Hooper to his table, where the good minister had blessed the food almost every Sunday since taking up his post. So he returned to the parsonage. As he closed the door, people saw him look back at them, all their eyes still fixed on him. A sad smile gleamed faintly beneath the veil, flickering around his mouth as he disappeared.
“How strange,” said a lady, “that a simple black veil, the kind any woman might wear on her bonnet, should become so dreadful on Mr. Hooper’s face!”

“Surely something is wrong with Mr. Hooper’s mind,” observed her husband, the village doctor. “But the strangest thing is how this odd behavior affects even a sensible man like me. Although the black veil covers only his face, its influence spreads over his whole body. It makes him ghostlike from head to foot. Don’t you feel that too?”
“I certainly do,” his wife replied. “I wouldn’t be alone with him for anything. I wonder he isn’t afraid to be alone with himself.”
“Men sometimes are,” her husband said.

The afternoon service passed in much the same way. Afterward, the bell tolled for a young woman’s funeral. Her family and friends had gathered in the house, and less intimate acquaintances stood by the door, speaking of her good qualities. Their conversation stopped when Mr. Hooper appeared, still wearing his black veil. Now it was an appropriate symbol. He entered the room where the body lay and bent over the coffin to say a last farewell to his dead parishioner. As he stooped, the veil hung straight down from his forehead. If the young woman’s eyelids had not been closed forever, she could have seen his face. Was he afraid of her gaze, that he so quickly pulled the black veil back into place? One person watching this meeting of the living and the dead did not hesitate to declare that, at the instant the minister’s face was exposed, the corpse shuddered slightly. Its shroud and muslin cap rustled, though its face retained death’s stillness. A superstitious old woman was the only witness to this marvel.

From the coffin, Mr. Hooper went into the room where the mourners waited, then to the top of the stairs to offer the funeral prayer. It was tender and heart-melting, full of sorrow, yet so filled with heavenly hope that a heavenly harp swept by the fingers of the dead seemed faintly audible within the minister’s saddest tones. The people trembled, though they understood him only dimly, when he prayed that they, he himself, and all humanity might be ready—as he trusted this young woman had been—for the dreadful hour that would tear the veil from their faces. The bearers walked heavily out, and the mourners followed, bringing sadness to the whole street, with the dead before them and Mr. Hooper in his black veil behind.
“Why are you looking back?” one person in the procession asked his companion.
“I imagined,” she replied, “that the minister and the young woman’s spirit were walking hand in hand.”
“So did I, at that very moment,” the other said.

That night, Milford’s most handsome couple were to be married. Though considered a melancholy man, Mr. Hooper had a calm cheerfulness on such occasions. It often drew an answering smile where livelier merriment would have failed. No other quality made him more beloved. The wedding guests impatiently awaited his arrival, hoping that the strange dread surrounding him all day would now disappear. But it did not. When he arrived, their eyes fell first on the same horrible black veil that had deepened the funeral’s gloom and could promise nothing but evil for the wedding. Its effect was immediate. A dark cloud seemed to roll from beneath the black crepe and dim the candles. The bride and groom stood before the minister, but her cold fingers trembled in his shaking hand. Her deathly paleness made people whisper that the young woman buried a few hours earlier had risen from her grave to be married. If any other wedding had ever been so dismal, it was that famous one where the wedding bell tolled like a funeral bell.

After the ceremony, Mr. Hooper raised a glass of wine to his lips and wished the newlyweds happiness with gentle humor. His words should have brightened the guests’ faces like a cheerful glow from the hearth. But at that instant he glimpsed his reflection in a mirror. The black veil filled his own soul with the horror it inspired in everyone else. His body shook, his lips turned white, and he spilled the untasted wine onto the carpet. He rushed into the darkness, for the Earth, too, wore her black veil.

The next day, Milford talked of almost nothing but Parson Hooper’s black veil. It and the mystery hidden behind it occupied acquaintances meeting in the street and good women gossiping at open windows. It was the first news the tavernkeeper told his guests. Children chattered about it on their way to school. One little mimic covered his face with an old black handkerchief. He frightened his playmates so badly that their panic seized him too, and his own joke almost drove him out of his mind.

Remarkably, not one of the parish’s busybodies or rude, intrusive people dared ask Mr. Hooper plainly why he was doing this. Until now, whenever there had been the slightest excuse to interfere, he had never lacked advisers, nor had he resisted being guided by their judgment. If he had a fault, it was such painful self-doubt that the mildest criticism could make him regard a harmless action as a crime. Yet, though they knew this gentle weakness so well, none of his parishioners chose to offer a friendly objection to the black veil. A feeling of dread, neither openly admitted nor carefully concealed, made each pass the responsibility to someone else. At last they decided to send church representatives to speak to him about the mystery before it became a scandal. No delegation ever performed its duty so poorly. The minister received them with friendly courtesy, but once they sat down, he fell silent. He left them the entire burden of introducing their important business. The subject should have been obvious enough. There was the black veil, wrapped around his forehead and hiding everything above his calm mouth, where they sometimes saw a sad smile glimmer. But in their imaginations that piece of crepe hung before his heart, the symbol of a fearful secret between him and them. If he would only lift it, they could speak freely about it—but not before. So they sat for a long time, speechless, confused, and shrinking uneasily from the gaze they felt fixed on them invisibly. At last they returned, ashamed, to those who had sent them. They declared the matter too serious for anything less than a council of churches, and perhaps it would even require a General Synod.

But one person in the village was untouched by the dread the black veil had inspired in everyone else. When the representatives returned without an explanation, without even daring to ask for one, she resolved with her usual calm determination to drive away the strange cloud gathering more darkly around Mr. Hooper every moment. As the woman engaged to marry him, she should have the right to know what the veil concealed. So, at the minister’s first visit, she brought up the subject with a direct simplicity that made it easier for both of them. After he sat down, she looked steadily at the veil. She could see none of the dreadful gloom that had overwhelmed the crowd. It was only two folds of crepe, hanging from his forehead to his mouth and stirring slightly with his breath.

“No,” she said aloud, smiling, “there is nothing dreadful in this piece of crepe, except that it hides a face I am always glad to see. Come, dear sir, let the sun shine from behind the cloud. First take off your black veil, then tell me why you put it on.”
Mr. Hooper’s smile glimmered faintly.
“A time is coming,” he said, “when all of us will cast aside our veils. Beloved friend, don’t take offense if I wear this piece of crepe until then.”
“Your words are a mystery too,” the young woman replied. “At least take the veil away from them.”

“Elizabeth, I will,” he said, “as far as my vow allows. Know, then, that this veil is an image and a symbol. I am bound to wear it always, in light and darkness, alone and before crowds, with strangers and with close friends. No mortal eye will ever see it removed. This gloomy covering must separate me from the world. Even you, Elizabeth, can never come behind it.”
“What terrible sorrow has come upon you,” she asked earnestly, “that you must darken your eyes forever like this?”
“If it is a sign of mourning,” Mr. Hooper replied, “perhaps, like most other mortals, I have sorrows dark enough for a black veil to represent.”

“But what if the world refuses to believe it represents an innocent sorrow?” Elizabeth insisted. “However loved and respected you are, people may whisper that you hide your face because you know yourself guilty of a secret sin. For the sake of your sacred calling, end this scandal.”

Her cheeks flushed as she hinted at the rumors already circulating in the village. But Mr. Hooper remained gentle. He even smiled again: the same sad smile that always seemed like a faint glimmer of light rising from the darkness beneath the veil.

“If I hide my face for sorrow, I have reason enough,” he simply answered. “And if I cover it for secret sin, what mortal might not do the same?” With this gentle but unbreakable stubbornness, he resisted all her pleas.

At last Elizabeth fell silent. For a few moments she seemed lost in thought, probably considering how else to draw her lover away from this dark fantasy. If it meant nothing else, perhaps it was a sign of mental illness. Though stronger in character than he was, she began to cry. Then, in what seemed an instant, another feeling replaced her sorrow. Her eyes had settled unconsciously on the black veil, and its terrors fell around her like sudden twilight. She rose and stood trembling before him.
“So at last you feel it too?” he said mournfully.
She did not answer. Covering her eyes with her hand, she turned to leave. He rushed forward and caught her arm.

“Be patient with me, Elizabeth!” he cried passionately. “Don’t abandon me, though this veil must stand between us here on earth. Be mine, and in the life to come there will be no veil over my face, no darkness between our souls. It is only a mortal veil, not one for eternity. Oh, you don’t know how lonely I am, how frightened to be alone behind my black veil! Don’t leave me forever in this miserable darkness.”
“Lift the veil just once and look me in the face,” she said.
“Never! It cannot be!” Mr. Hooper replied.
“Then goodbye!” said Elizabeth.

She pulled her arm from his grasp and slowly left. At the door she paused for one long, shuddering look that seemed almost to penetrate the mystery of the black veil. Yet even in his grief, Mr. Hooper smiled at the thought that a mere physical symbol had separated him from happiness, although the horrors it represented must hang darkly between even the most loving couples.

After that, no one tried to remove Mr. Hooper’s veil or directly ask about the secret it supposedly hid. People who claimed to be above common prejudice dismissed it as an eccentric whim, the sort that often mixes with the sensible behavior of otherwise rational men and colors it all with an appearance of madness. But to everyone else, good Mr. Hooper had become an enduring figure of terror. He could not walk peacefully down the street. He knew that gentle, timid people would turn away to avoid him, while others would deliberately put themselves in his path to show their courage. The latter group’s rudeness forced him to abandon his usual sunset walk to the graveyard. Whenever he leaned thoughtfully over its gate, faces would peer from behind the gravestones at his black veil. A story spread that the dead people’s stares had driven him away. It grieved him to the depths of his kind heart to see children flee when he approached, abandoning their happiest games while his mournful figure was still far off. More than anything else, their instinctive fear made him feel that supernatural horror was woven into the threads of the black crepe. Indeed, his own dislike of the veil was known to be so strong that he never willingly passed a mirror or bent to drink from a still fountain, afraid his reflection in its peaceful surface would frighten him. This gave weight to whispers that his conscience tortured him for some great crime too horrible to hide completely or hint at except in this obscure way. From beneath the veil, a cloud rolled into the sunshine: an uncertainty of sin or sorrow that surrounded the poor minister and kept love and sympathy from reaching him. People said ghosts and demons kept him company there. Shuddering at himself and surrounded by outward terrors, he walked continually in its shadow, groping in the darkness of his own soul or looking through a covering that saddened the whole world. Even the unruly wind, people believed, respected his dreadful secret and never blew the veil aside. Yet good Mr. Hooper still smiled sadly at the crowd’s pale, worldly faces as he passed.

Among all its harmful effects, the black veil did one good thing: it made its wearer a very effective minister. Through his mysterious symbol, for no other cause was apparent, he gained an awesome power over souls tormented by sin. His converts always regarded him with a special dread of their own. They said, though only figuratively, that before he brought them into heavenly light, they had been with him behind the black veil. Its darkness did enable him to understand every dark feeling. Dying sinners cried out for Mr. Hooper and would not breathe their last until he came. Yet whenever he bent to whisper comfort, they shuddered at the veiled face so close to theirs. Such was the terror of the black veil, even when Death had uncovered his own face. Strangers traveled long distances to attend his church simply to stare at his figure, since they could not see his face. But many were trembling before they left. Once, during Governor Belcher’s administration, Mr. Hooper was chosen to preach the election sermon. Wearing his black veil, he stood before the chief magistrate, council, and representatives. He made such a deep impression that the laws passed that year carried all the gloom and religious devotion of our earliest ancestors’ rule.

In this way Mr. Hooper lived a long life, blameless in his outward conduct but wrapped in gloomy suspicions. He was kind and loving, yet unloved and vaguely feared; a man set apart from others, avoided in their health and happiness but always summoned to help them in their mortal anguish. As the passing years scattered their snow above his black veil, his name spread through the New England churches. They called him Father Hooper. Nearly all the parishioners who had been adults when he first arrived had been carried away in one funeral after another. He had one congregation inside the church and a larger one in the churchyard. Having worked so late into the evening, and done his work so well, good Father Hooper’s turn to rest had come.

Shaded candlelight revealed several people in the old minister’s death room. He had no family. But the doctor was there, properly solemn though unmoved, seeking only to ease the last pains of a patient he could not save. There were deacons and other deeply religious members of his church. The Reverend Mr. Clark of Westbury, a young, zealous minister, had ridden there in haste to pray at the dying man’s bedside. There was the nurse—not a paid servant of Death, but someone whose quiet love had endured all these years in secrecy, loneliness, and the chill of old age, and would not die even at the hour of death. Who could it be but Elizabeth! And there lay good Father Hooper’s white-haired head on his deathbed pillow, the black veil still wrapped around his forehead and falling over his face, stirred by every increasingly difficult gasp of his faint breath. All his life that piece of crepe had hung between him and the world. It had separated him from cheerful fellowship and a woman’s love, keeping him in that saddest of prisons, his own heart. Still it covered his face, as though to deepen his dark room’s gloom and shade him from eternity’s sunshine.

For some time his mind had been confused, wandering uncertainly between past and present, and at intervals seeming to hover forward into the indistinct world to come. Feverish spells tossed him from side to side and wore away his little remaining strength. Yet even in his most violent convulsions and wildest mental wanderings, when no other thought retained its steady influence, he showed a terrible anxiety that the black veil might slip aside. Even if his bewildered soul could have forgotten, a faithful woman sat at his pillow. With her eyes turned away, she would have covered the aged face she had last seen in the handsome years of his manhood.

At last the dying old man lay quiet, dulled by exhaustion of mind and body. His pulse could not be felt. His breath grew fainter and fainter, except when a long, deep, uneven gasp seemed to announce that his spirit was about to take flight.
The minister from Westbury approached the bed.
“Revered Father Hooper,” he said, “the moment of your release is near. Are you ready for the lifting of the veil that separates time from eternity?”
At first Father Hooper answered only with a weak movement of his head. Then, perhaps afraid that his meaning was unclear, he made an effort to speak.
“Yes,” he said faintly. “My soul waits patiently, but wearily, for that veil to be lifted.”

“And is it right,” the Reverend Mr. Clark continued, “that a man so devoted to prayer, so blameless an example, holy in thought and deed as far as human judgment can tell—is it right that a father of the Church should leave a shadow on his memory that might seem to stain so pure a life? I beg you, my revered brother, don’t let this happen. Let us rejoice in your triumphant face as you go to your reward. Before eternity’s veil is lifted, let me remove this black veil from your face.” As he spoke, Mr. Clark leaned forward to uncover the mystery of so many years.

But with a sudden burst of strength that horrified everyone watching, Father Hooper pulled both hands from under the bedclothes and pressed them firmly against the black veil. He was determined to struggle if the Westbury minister was willing to fight a dying man.
“Never!” the veiled minister cried. “On earth, never!”
“Dark old man!” the frightened minister exclaimed. “With what horrible crime on your soul are you going to judgment?”

Father Hooper’s breath heaved and rattled in his throat. Yet with a mighty effort, reaching forward with his hands, he caught hold of life and held it back until he could speak. He even raised himself in bed. There he sat, shivering in Death’s arms, while the black veil hung down, dreadful in that final moment with all the gathered terrors of a lifetime. Yet the faint, sad smile so often seen there seemed to glimmer from its darkness and linger on his lips.

“Why do you tremble at me alone?” he cried, turning his veiled face around the circle of pale onlookers. “Tremble at each other too. Have men avoided me, women shown no pity, and children screamed and fled only because of my black veil? What makes this piece of crepe so dreadful except the mystery it dimly represents? When friend shows friend what lies deepest in the heart, and the lover does the same for the beloved; when people no longer shrink uselessly from their Creator’s eye, disgustingly hoarding the secrets of their sins—then call me a monster for the symbol beneath which I have lived and am dying. I look around me, and see a black veil on every face!”

As his listeners shrank from one another in shared terror, Father Hooper fell back onto his pillow, a veiled corpse with a faint smile lingering on his lips. Still veiled, they laid him in his coffin. Still veiled, they carried him to his grave. The grass of many years has grown and withered there. Moss covers the gravestone, and good Mr. Hooper’s face is dust. Yet the thought that it decayed beneath the black veil remains dreadful.
